opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a few things have gone better than I would have guessed, say, five or ten years ago.

The biggest one is that we've ended up with AI systems that are, in a sense, trained on human language and human thought. Large language models learn by absorbing an enormous amount of text that people have written. That means the path to powerful AI is running through systems that, at least on the surface, understand human concepts, can talk to us in natural language, and can explain what they're doing, at least sort of. If you go back to the older picture of how AI might develop, a lot of people imagined something closer to a pure reinforcement learning agent: a system that just optimizes some score in an environment and develops very alien internal goals and representations. That's scarier, because it's much harder to communicate with, inspect, or steer.

A second thing is that progress has been fairly gradual and visible, in the sense that we're getting a lot of intermediate systems along the way. We have models that are useful, that people interact with every day, that researchers can study, poke at, red-team, and run experiments on. That gives us a chance to learn about alignment empirically rather than having to get everything right in theory before we ever see the thing. Some of the scariest scenarios involved a sudden jump from not-very-capable to extremely capable with no warning, and so far it looks more like a steady ramp with lots of opportunities to notice problems.

Third, I think there's real potential for AI to help with the problem itself. If you have systems that are quite capable at research, coding, and analysis, but not yet so capable that they're uncontrollable, there's a window where you might be able to use them to accelerate alignment research, interpretability, security, and so on. That's not guaranteed to work, and it's a big part of what I worry about getting right, but the shape of the technology makes it more plausible than it would otherwise be.

And then, related, things like chain-of-thought reasoning, where models think out loud in language before answering, give us at least some window into their reasoning. It's imperfect, it may not be fully faithful, and it might not last if training practices change. But it's an opportunity that I don't think people would have predicted.

Now, I want to be careful. None of this means the risk is low. There are still big concerns: models could learn to deceive, we might see situational awareness and strategic behavior that undermines the evaluations we rely on, competitive pressure could push developers to cut corners, and the whole thing is moving very fast. But relative to the range of ways this could have gone, the specific trajectory we're on has a number of features that make me think the problem is more tractable than it could have been. And that's a big part of why I think it's worth working on intensely right now, because there's a real shot at making it go well.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a sudden jump from not-very-capable to extremely capable with the gradual progress and intermediate systems observed so far.

r002.rationale: It describes a window to study, red-team, and run alignment experiments on useful AI systems before they become uncontrollable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people were surprised by this — I was surprised by this — but the way AI has actually developed has been a lot more gradual and a lot more legible than the scenario I used to spend most of my time worrying about.

So if you go back to, say, 2015 or 2016, the picture that a lot of us had in our heads was something like: you've got systems that aren't very impressive, aren't very impressive, aren't very impressive, and then there's some kind of discontinuity where a system becomes radically more capable than anything that came before, maybe through recursive self-improvement, and you basically get one shot. You've got to have solved alignment in advance, with no real-world feedback, for a system you've never seen, with properties you can only guess at. And that's a really hard problem. That's the kind of problem where I think pessimism is warranted.

What's actually happened is that we've gotten these systems that are enormously capable in some ways, and they came out in public, and lots of people use them, and we get to see what they do. We get to see how they fail. We get to run evaluations on them. We get to do interpretability research on them. And each generation is noticeably better than the last, but not so much better that the whole world flips overnight. So you end up in this regime where you have a lot of iterations to learn from, and you can actually study the thing you're worried about rather than theorizing about it.

And I think that changes a lot. One thing it changes is that the research community can be empirical. Instead of arguing from first principles about what a superintelligence would want, you can ask, "OK, does this model behave deceptively under these conditions? Can we detect it? Does this training method make it better or worse?" Those are questions you can actually make progress on, and people are making progress on them.

Another thing it changes is the political and institutional side. It was always going to be really hard to get governments and companies to take seriously a risk from a technology that didn't exist yet and that sounded like science fiction. It's a lot easier when there are products that hundreds of millions of people use, and when the people building them are saying in public, "Yeah, we think this could be dangerous." You've seen companies put out safety frameworks, you've seen governments set up institutes to evaluate models — none of that is sufficient, but it's a lot more than I would have predicted even a few years ago, and I think it's downstream of the technology being visible and incremental.

A third thing — and this one I think is underrated — is that we're getting a lot more useful AI before we get the really dangerous AI. So we can potentially use these systems to help with the safety problem itself: to help with alignment research, to help with monitoring, to help with evaluating other models. If the capabilities had arrived all at once, you wouldn't get that window.

Now, I want to be careful here. None of this means I think the risk is low. I still think there's a very real chance this goes badly. The trajectory could still speed up. The gradualness we've had so far is not guaranteed to continue. And "legible" doesn't mean "solved" — there are plenty of things these models do that we can't explain. But the shape of the problem looks more tractable to me than the shape I was imagining a decade ago. It looks like a hard engineering and governance problem with feedback loops, rather than a one-shot philosophy problem with no feedback at all. And I'd much rather be working on the first kind.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the feared sudden jump from unimpressive systems to radically more capable ones with observed gradual, incremental progress and repeated opportunities to learn.

r002.rationale: It describes time to study capable systems before “really dangerous AI,” but does not communicate that this window is before systems become too capable for humans to catch their problematic behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is that AI progress has become a lot more concrete. When I first started worrying about this, a lot of the conversation was necessarily very abstract: imagine a future system that’s enormously powerful, and then try to reason about what could go wrong and what you could do about it. That’s a hard way to make progress, and it’s a hard way to get people engaged.

Now we have systems that are impressive enough that more people can see why this might matter, but that also give us something to study. You can try different approaches to getting a model to behave the way you want. You can look for dangerous capabilities. You can investigate whether your safety measures actually work. That creates the possibility of an empirical research field, with feedback loops, rather than just a debate about hypothetical future systems.

And there’s at least the possibility that AI itself helps us do that research. I wouldn’t want to assume that works out, because relying on an AI to help make AI safe raises its own questions. But it’s a potentially important advantage.

So I wouldn’t say that more impressive capabilities are straightforwardly good news. They also make the risks more pressing. What gives me hope is that we’re getting opportunities to learn and to build a serious response while there’s still something we can do about it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI progress is more concrete and enables empirical research, but it does not argue that observed progress contradicts AI rapidly passing through intermediate intelligence levels.

r002.rationale: The response mentions opportunities to learn while there is still something we can do, but it does not identify an extended window before systems become too capable for humans to catch problematic behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing that’s made me more hopeful is that AI progress has become much more visible and concrete. A few years ago, it was harder to get people to engage with the possibility of very powerful AI. Now people can interact with these systems and see both how impressive they are and how strange their failures can be. That makes it easier to have a serious conversation about where this could be heading.

There’s also a potentially encouraging feature of the trajectory itself: we’re getting systems that are useful and worth studying before they’re capable of the most dangerous things we’re worried about. That gives us opportunities to do empirical safety research, learn how to evaluate models, and build up experience with what works and what doesn’t. If you had imagined that AI would look unimpressive right up until some sudden breakthrough produced something enormously powerful, this looks like a better situation for learning and responding.

And the systems themselves may become useful for safety work—for helping us understand other AI systems, find problems, and develop better safeguards. I wouldn’t want to assume that happens automatically, or that we can safely hand the whole problem over to them. But it’s a possibility that seems more concrete than it used to.

So I’m still very concerned. Progress also means we may have less time. But I can see more of a path now from the systems we have to the research, institutions, and public understanding we’d need to handle this well.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts useful, studyable systems appearing before dangerous capability with the imagined scenario of AI staying unimpressive until a sudden breakthrough to enormous power.

r002.rationale: It describes opportunities to study safety before systems reach the most dangerous capabilities, but does not identify a window before systems become too capable for humans to catch their problematic behavior.
